title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Decision on Amending the Provisions on the Causes of Action in Civil Cases
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Notice on Issuing the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action in Civil Cases

Fa [2025] No. 227

High People's Courts of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government; the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; the Production and Construction Corps Branch of the High People's Court of Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region:

To implement the spirit of the Fourth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, focus on the main objectives of economic and social development during the "Fifteenth Five-Year Plan" period, and fulfill the requirement of Article 29 of the Sixth Five-Year Reform Outline for People's Courts (2024-2028) to "improve and refine the case, case number, and cause of action systems, as well as the precise identification work mechanism," the Supreme People's Court has revised the Provisions on Causes of Action in Civil Cases (hereinafter referred to as the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action), which were last amended on December 29, 2020. These revised provisions shall come into effect on January 1, 2026. The revised Provisions on Causes of Action in Civil Cases (hereinafter referred to as the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action) are hereby issued to you for earnest implementation.

Since the implementation of the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action, they have played an important role in facilitating parties in initiating civil proceedings and standardizing the work of people's courts in civil case filing, adjudication, and judicial statistics. In recent years, with the enactment or amendment of laws such as the Law on the Protection of the Status and Rights and Interests of Military Personnel, the Work Safety Law, the Personal Information Protection Law, the Seed Law, the Anti-Monopoly Law, the Law on the Protection of Women's Rights and Interests, the Civil Procedure Law, the Company Law, the Law on Rural Collective Economic Organizations, the Mineral Resources Law, the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, the Arbitration Law, and the Maritime Law, many new types of civil disputes have emerged in judicial practice, necessitating supplements and improvements to the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. Following in-depth investigation, research, and extensive solicitation of opinions, the Supreme People's Court has revised the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. The following is hereby notified to people's courts at all levels regarding the application of the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action:

I. Attach High Importance to the Important Role of Causes of Action in Civil Cases in the Standardization of Civil Adjudication, and Diligently Study and Master the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action

A civil cause of action is an important component of a civil case name. It reflects the nature of the civil legal relationship involved in the case, summarizes the nature of the legal relationship in dispute between the parties, and serves as an important tool for people's courts in managing civil cases. Establishing a scientific and comprehensive system of civil causes of action is conducive to facilitating parties in initiating civil proceedings, unifying the standards for the application of law in civil cases, classifying and managing accepted cases, determining the jurisdictional division among various civil adjudication divisions, and enhancing the accuracy and scientific nature of judicial statistics for civil cases. This, in turn, serves to better innovate and strengthen civil adjudication management, support the judicial decision-making of people's courts, and promote the improvement of quality and efficiency in civil adjudication work.

People's courts at all levels shall diligently study the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action, understand the structure of the cause of action system, and the background, legal basis, determination standards, specific meanings, order of application, and methods for changing specific causes of action. They shall accurately select and apply the specific cause of action, legally protect the litigant rights of parties, innovate and strengthen civil adjudication management, and continuously advance the standardization of civil adjudication work.

II. Principles Followed in Revising the Provisions on Causes of Action

First, the principle of strict legality. All causes of action revised this time have a basis in substantive and procedural law and comply with the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law concerning the scope of acceptance of civil cases.

Second, the principle of necessity. This revision is premised on maintaining the stability of the existing cause of action operational system. Corresponding amendments are made only for causes of action that must be added or adjusted. Some specific causes of action are improved based on current legislative and judicial practice needs, without making major adjustments to the cause of action classification system.

Third, the principle of practicality. The cause of action system is organized based on existing valid legal provisions, fully considering the needs of people's courts for civil case filing, adjudication practice, and judicial statistics. This revision places greater emphasis on the conciseness, clarity, and practicality of causes of action, making them easy for parties to initiate civil proceedings and for people's courts to conduct civil case filing, adjudication, and judicial statistics work.

III. Standards for Determining Causes of Action

A civil cause of action shall be determined based on the nature of the civil legal relationship in dispute between the parties. Given that a specific case may involve multiple claims by the parties and multiple focal points of dispute, and the subject matter of the dispute may also be multiple, to ensure high-level summary and conciseness of the cause of action, the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action continue to adopt the determination standards used in the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. First, the expression of a civil cause of action is, in principle, determined as "Nature of Legal Relationship + Dispute," generally not including elements such as the focus of dispute, subject matter, or method of infringement. Second, considering the complex and variable nature of the civil legal relationships in dispute in practice, relying solely on the standard of legal relationship to classify the cause of action system cannot adequately meet the needs of civil adjudication practice or judicial statistics. Therefore, while adhering to the nature of the legal relationship as the primary standard for determining causes of action, for a small number of causes of action, other standards such as the right of claim, the right of formation, actions for confirmation, or actions for formation are also used. For a small number of causes of action, the expression also includes elements such as the focus of dispute, subject matter, or method of infringement. Third, to clearly distinguish from causes of action in administrative cases, special treatment is given to the expression of individual causes of action. Fourth, for cases heard under non-contentious procedures provided for by the Civil Procedure Law, such as special procedures, supervision procedures, public summons procedures, company liquidation, and bankruptcy procedures, the cause of action is directly stated based on the litigant's claims. Fifth, for cases under special procedures such as public interest litigation, third-party opposition proceedings, and objection proceedings in enforcement procedures, the cause of action is directly stated based on the litigation system provided for by the amended Civil Procedure Law.

IV. Overall Organization of the Cause of Action System

1. Regarding the vertical and horizontal organization of the cause of action system. The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action are based on the classification of civil legal relationships in civil law theory and organize the vertical system of causes of action according to the content of legal relationships, namely the types of civil rights. Vertically, combined with civil legislation such as the Civil Code and the Civil Procedure Law, and adjudication practice, the cause of action classification system is divided into the following twelve major parts, serving as the first-level causes of action: Personality Rights Disputes; Marriage, Family, and Inheritance Disputes; Property Rights Disputes; Contract and Quasi-Contract Disputes; Intellectual Property and Competition Disputes; Data and Online Virtual Property Disputes; Labor Disputes, Personnel Disputes, and New Employment Form Labor Disputes; Maritime and Admiralty Disputes; Civil Disputes Related to Companies, Securities, Insurance, Negotiable Instruments, etc.; Tort Liability Disputes; Causes of Action for Non-Contentious Procedure Cases; and Causes of Action for Special Litigation Procedure Cases.

Horizontally, through the design of a total-subordinate four-level structure, the evolution of causes of action from higher (general) to lower (specific) levels is achieved. For example: Property Rights Disputes (First-Level Cause of Action) → Ownership Disputes (Second-Level Cause of Action) → Building Distinction Ownership Disputes (Third-Level Cause of Action) → Owner's Exclusive Right Disputes (Fourth-Level Cause of Action). Under the first-level causes of action, there are fifty-nine categories of second-level causes of action (indicated by uppercase Chinese numerals). Under the second-level causes of action, there are 514 third-level causes of action (indicated by Arabic numerals). Third-level causes of action are the most common and widely used in judicial practice. Based on the needs of adjudication guidance, research, and judicial statistics, 470 fourth-level causes of action (indicated by Arabic numerals in parentheses) are listed under some third-level causes of action. Due to the complexity of civil legal relationships, it is impossible to exhaust all fourth-level causes of action; the currently listed fourth-level causes of action are only some typical, common, or established ones for judicial statistical needs.

The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action adopt a vertical structure of twelve parts and a horizontal structure of four levels, forming a network-like structural system that essentially covers the types of civil dispute cases involved in the Civil Code and those currently accepted by people's courts. This facilitates the implementation of provisions in the Civil Code and other civil laws concerning the protection of civil rights and interests.

2. Regarding the organization of property rights disputes causes of action and contract disputes causes of action. The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action continue to follow the organizational structure of property rights disputes causes of action and contract disputes causes of action in the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. According to the principle of separating the cause and effect of changes in property rights, for causes of action in disputes arising from the cause of changes in property rights, i.e., contractual relationships of a creditor's right nature, the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action still place them under Contract Disputes. For causes of action in disputes arising from the effect of changes in property rights, i.e., property relationships resulting from the establishment, ownership, validity, use, and income of property rights, the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action still place them under Property Rights Disputes.

In specific application, the people's court shall determine the nature of the legal relationship in dispute between the parties and ascertain whether this legal relationship involves the cause or the effect of changes in property rights to correctly determine the cause of action. If the nature of the legal relationship in dispute involves the cause of changes in property rights (i.e., disputes arising from contractual relationships of a creditor's right nature), the cause of action under the second-level cause of action "Contract Disputes" should be selected, such as "Right of Habitation Contract Disputes." If the nature of the legal relationship in dispute involves the effect of changes in property rights (i.e., disputes arising from property relationships such as the establishment, ownership, validity, use, and income of property rights), the cause of action under the first-level cause of action "Property Rights Disputes" should be selected, such as "Right of Habitation Disputes."

3. Regarding the organization of causes of action under "Property Rights Protection Disputes" and "Ownership Disputes," "Usufructuary Rights Disputes," and "Security Interests Disputes" within Part III "Property Rights Disputes." The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action continue to follow the organization of property rights disputes causes of action in the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. The causes of action "Ownership Disputes," "Usufructuary Rights Disputes," and "Security Interests Disputes" include both causes of action for confirmation of the above three types of property rights and causes of action for infringement of the above three types of property rights. The methods of protection provided in Chapter III "Protection of Property Rights" of the Property Rights Book of the Civil Code, namely property rights claims or creditor's rights claims (i.e., "Property Rights Protection Disputes"), may apply, in whole or in part, under each type of property right (third-level cause of action) listed in the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action. Most can be listed as fourth-level causes of action. However, to avoid making the entire cause of action system lengthy and cumbersome, they are not listed individually under each third-level cause of action. In practice, when determining the cause of action for a specific case, if the litigant's claims only involve one type of property rights claim or creditor's rights claim under "Property Rights Protection Disputes," the third-level cause of action under "Property Rights Protection Disputes" may be selected. If the litigant's claims involve two or more types of property rights claims or creditor's rights claims under "Property Rights Protection Disputes," then, depending on the type of right being protected, the third-level cause of action under "Ownership Disputes," "Usufructuary Rights Disputes," or "Security Interests Disputes" (various types of property rights disputes) should be selected.

4. Regarding the organization of tort liability disputes causes of action. The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action continue to follow the organizational structure of tort liability disputes causes of action and other first-level causes of action in the 2020 Provisions on Causes of Action. According to the relevant provisions of the Tort Liability Book of the Civil Code, the object of protection of this Book is civil rights and interests, the specific scope of which is the personal and property rights and interests stipulated in Chapter V of the General Part of the Civil Code. These civil rights and interests are further detailed in the Personality Rights Book, the Property Rights Book, the Marriage and Family Book, and the Inheritance Book. Disputes over these civil rights and interests often involve both right confirmation disputes and tort liability disputes, increasing the difficulty of scientifically and reasonably organizing the civil cause of action system. To maintain the integrity and stability of the entire cause of action system and avoid duplication and overlap as much as possible, the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action retain the tort liability dispute causes of action for these infringed civil rights and interests under the first-level cause of action systems such as "Personality Rights Disputes," "Marriage, Family, and Inheritance Disputes," "Property Rights Disputes," "Intellectual Property and Competition Disputes," and "Data and Online Virtual Property Disputes." The causes of action under the first-level cause of action "Tort Liability Disputes" are adjusted in accordance with the new provisions of the Tort Liability Book. Additionally, some tort liability dispute causes of action that are common in practice, have special provisions in the Civil Code or other laws, or are inconvenient to list under other first-level causes of action are also listed under the first-level cause of action "Tort Liability Disputes," such as "Non-Motor Vehicle Traffic Accident Liability Disputes." For "catch-all" considerations, the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action places the first-level cause of action "Tort Liability Disputes" after the other nine civil rights and interests dispute types, as the tenth part.

In specific application, for disputes involving tort liability, to clarify and unify the application of law, the specific cause of action listed under Part X "Tort Liability Disputes" based on the relevant provisions of the Tort Liability Book should be applied first. If there is no corresponding cause of action, then specific causes of action under other parts such as "Personality Rights Disputes," "Property Rights Disputes," "Intellectual Property and Competition Disputes," and "Data and Online Virtual Property Disputes" should be applied. For example, environmental pollution and ultra-hazardous activities may both cause personal injury and property damage. When determining the cause of action, the causes of action "Environmental Pollution Liability Disputes" and "Ultra-Hazardous Activity Liability Disputes" under Part X "Tort Liability Disputes" should be applied. The causes of action "Life, Body, and Health Rights Disputes" under Part I "Personality Rights Disputes" or "Property Damage Compensation Disputes" under Part III "Property Rights Disputes" should not be applied.

V. Issues to Note When Applying the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action

1. In the horizontal cause of action system, the cause of action for an individual case shall be selected in order from lower to higher levels. When determining the cause of action for an individual case, the fourth-level cause of action shall be applied with priority. If there is no corresponding fourth-level cause of action, the relevant third-level cause of action shall be applied. If there is no provision in the third-level cause of action, the relevant second-level cause of action shall be applied. If there is no provision in the second-level cause of action, the relevant first-level cause of action shall be applied. This approach is conducive to more accurately reflecting the nature of the legal relationship in dispute between the parties, promoting scientific management by classification, and improving the accuracy of judicial statistics.

2. Regarding changes to the cause of action in individual cases. During the civil case filing review stage, the people's court may determine the corresponding cause of action for the individual case based on the nature of the legal relationship involved in the plaintiff's claims. After accepting a civil case, if upon trial it is found that a lower-level cause of action is applicable, the people's court shall correspondingly change the cause of action for the individual case. If upon trial it is found that the legal relationship on which the party based the lawsuit is inconsistent with the legal relationship actually in dispute, upon conclusion of the case, the cause of action for the individual case shall be correspondingly changed based on the nature of the legal relationship actually existing between the parties as ascertained by the court. If a party adds or changes its claims during the proceedings, causing a change in the legal relationship in dispute, the cause of action for the individual case shall be correspondingly changed.

3. Determining the cause of action in individual cases involving multiple legal relationships. If a single lawsuit involves two or more legal relationships, the cause of action for the individual case shall be determined based on the nature of the legal relationship(s) in dispute between the parties. If all are legal relationships in dispute, the corresponding causes of action shall be determined side-by-side according to the two or more legal relationships in dispute.

4. Determining the cause of action in individual cases involving a concurrence of claims. In the case of concurrence of claims, the people's court shall determine the corresponding cause of action based on the nature of the legal relationship involved in the claim that the party independently chooses to exercise.

5. Method of using selective causes of action in the cause of action system (i.e., some causes of action containing a Chinese comma/division mark). For these causes of action, the corresponding cause of action for the individual case shall be determined based on the specific facts of the case; the entire cause of action should not be directly quoted. For example, for the cause of action "Life, Body, and Health Rights Disputes," the corresponding cause of action shall be determined based on the specific object of infringement.

6. Correctly understanding the nature and function of civil causes of action. The organization and formulation of the cause of action system is a means for people's courts to manage civil adjudication. People's courts at all levels shall, in accordance with the law, protect the right of parties to file lawsuits as provided by law. The Revised Provisions on Causes of Action shall not be equated with the conditions for filing a lawsuit stipulated in Article 122 of the Civil Procedure Law. A court shall not rule to dismiss a case or reject a lawsuit on the grounds that there is no corresponding cause of action in the Revised Provisions on Causes of Action for the party's claim, thereby harming the party's right to litigate.

This revision of civil case causes of action is primarily based on the current judicial practice experience of people's courts, aligning with legislative revisions to improve and perfect relevant specific causes of action. Local people's courts at all levels shall, in light of new situations and new problems encountered in case filing and adjudication, focus on summarizing and reporting new types of cases for which it is indeed necessary to add or modify corresponding causes of action, and promptly report them level by level to the Supreme People's Court.

December 16, 2025

Provisions on Causes of Action in Civil Cases
